bib.title: Atlas: Few-shot Learning with Retrieval Augmented Language Models

legacy_report:
I read the whole Atlas paper. One thing matters most for your note: Atlas's "few-shot" results come from fine-tuning on the 64 examples, while PaLM, Chinchilla, Gopher and GPT-3 were prompted in-context. The 42.4 vs 39.6 comparison is therefore not like-for-like on method.

SOURCE: Atlas: Few-shot Learning with Retrieval Augmented Language Models. Izacard, Lewis, Lomeli, Hosseini, Petroni, Schick, Dwivedi-Yu, Joulin, Riedel, Grave (Meta AI Research). Preprint, arXiv 2208.03299v3, 16 Nov 2022.

COVERAGE: All 120,635 extracted characters across 33 pages (page markers added). The main text, all tables and Appendix A (pp. 27–33: MMLU details, inter-run variance, per-domain Tables 16–18, QA scaling Table 19, KILT dev Table 20) were read in full. The references (about chars 80k–90.7k) were skimmed only for where methods came from.

CLAIMS
- claim: An 11B retrieval-augmented model beats the 540B PaLM on 64-shot NaturalQuestions by almost 3 points.
  number: 42.4 EM vs 39.6 (45.1 with a Wikipedia-only index)
  setup: Atlas-11B (T5-XXL Fusion-in-Decoder reader plus a BERT-base Contriever retriever), fine-tuned on 64 examples for 30 steps with query-side retriever fine-tuning. It retrieves 40 passages (Appendix A.2.1) from the default index, CCNet plus the Dec 2021 Wikipedia. Baselines use prompting, not fine-tuning (Table 8 caption: "For the 64-shot setting, our model uses fine-tuning, while the other models use prompting.").
  quote: "with only 11B parameters,Atlasachieves an accuracy of 42.4% on NaturalQuestions using 64 training examples (45.1% with a Wikipedia-only index), outperforming PaLM (Chowdhery et al., 2022), a 540B parameter model by almost 3 points, and 64.0% in a full-dataset setting with a Wikipedia index, establishing a new state of the art by 8 points." Table 8: "PaLM (Chowdhery et al., 2022) 39.6 ... Atlas 42.4 60.4 74.5 79.8 84.7 89.4"
  where: p.2; Table 8 p.14
- claim: The 45.1 figure uses the Dec 2018 Wikipedia dump. That dump is temporally matched to when NQ was collected and gives the best NQ score.
  number: 64-shot 44.7/45.1/44.1/44.0/41.3 and full 63.2/64.0/62.4/61.1/59.6 for the Dec 2017 / Dec 2018 / Aug 2019 / Dec 2020 / Dec 2021 dumps
  setup: Atlas-11B on NQ with the index swapped at fine-tuning time
  quote: "We observe that the 2018 December Wikipedia dump, which is close to the date of data collection, leads to the best results for both few-shot and full fine-tuning. In particular, it leads to a new state-of-the-art of 64 EM on NaturalQuestions."
  where: p.17; Table 12 p.18
- claim: Swapping the index at test time updates the answers without any retraining. A closed-book model cannot do this.
  number: Atlas trained on 2017 answers: 57.7 on 2017 with the 2017 index, 53.1 on 2020 with the 2020 index. Closed-book T5 scores 12.1 and 2.9.
  setup: TempLAMA-derived cloze set of 248 train / 112 dev / 806 test questions whose answer changes between 2017 and 2020. Models are Atlas-11B and T5-11B (called T5-XXL in the text).
  quote: "we can swap the Atlas index to a 2020 Wikipedia index,without retraining, and find thatAtlas updates its predictions accordingly, with 2020 accuracy rising to a similar level to its 2017 performance (53.1%), whereas the purely parametric T5 has no such updateability mechanism."
  where: p.17; Table 11 p.18
- claim: Updating works backwards in time too. A closed-book model trained on 2020 answers still fails on 2020 questions.
  number: 50.1 (Atlas, 2020-trained, 2017 index); 3.6 (T5)
  setup: as above
  quote: "demonstrate Atlascan zero-shot transfer backwards in time to 2017 effectively too (50.1%). Interestingly, T5 is unable answer questions from 2020 well, even when trained with 2020 answers (3.6%)"
  where: p.17
- claim: The four retriever losses show no systematic difference. PDist was chosen for stability and cost, and joint pre-training matters mostly for the language model.
  number: 64-shot average: Fixed retriever 42.2, ADist 43.0, EMDR2 43.3, PDist 45.7, LOOP 43.7, no joint pre-training 30.0, closed-book 26.5. 1024-shot averages: 51.1 / 51.4 / 49.6 / 51.0 / 50.8.
  setup: T5-XL 3B, MLM pre-training for 10k steps, Dec 2021 Wikipedia for both index and pre-training data. Evaluated on NQ, WoW and FEVER from KILT.
  quote: "we do not observe significant systematic differences between the different retriever training objectives. We thus decide adopt use Perplexity Distillation for subsequent experiments, as it tends to be more stable than EMDR2 or ADist, and more computationally efficient than LOOP." Also: "This effect tends to be less marked on 64-shot downstream tasks, and almost non-existent for 1024-shot. We believe that this is evidence that the biggest impact of pre-training is on the language model"
  where: Table 1 p.10; text p.11
- claim: Refreshing the full index during joint training costs about 30% extra compute. Re-ranking a larger candidate set costs about 10%. Query-side fine-tuning costs nothing.
  number: ~30%; 10%
  setup: 37M-passage Wikipedia index, batch 64, 20 documents, refresh every 1000 steps; BERT-base retriever with a T5-XL reader. L = 10×K for re-ranking.
  quote: "this results in an overhead of∼ 30%." / "If we re-rank 10x more documents than what the language model processes (i.e.,L = 10×K), we get an overhead of10%."
  where: p.6
- claim: A frozen retriever during fine-tuning hurts. Query-side fine-tuning is best at 64 shots, and full fine-tuning is better at 1024.
  number: 64-shot average: standard 44.1, top-100 re-rank 44.7, query-side 45.7, fixed 41.1. 1024-shot average: 51.7 / 51.6 / 51.0 / 48.3.
  setup: 3B ablation, Table 4
  quote: "in the 64-shot setup, this is slightly stronger than performing full fine-tuning, which we attribute to there being less opportunity for over-fitting. On the other hand, on the 1024-shot setting, performing a full fine-tuning leads to stronger results"
  where: p.12
- claim: Retrieval beats a closed-book model of the same size on MMLU at every scale.
  number: +6.6 to +15.6 points
  setup: 770M, 3B and 11B models; 5-shot, 5-shot multitask and full/transfer settings; closed-book T5 trained on the same pre-training data
  quote: "Atlasoutperforms the closed-book baselines by between 6.6 and 15.6 points"
  where: p.12, Table 5
- claim: On MMLU 5-shot, Atlas-11B beats GPT-3 with 15x fewer parameters and 10x less pre-training compute.
  number: 47.9 vs 43.9; Train FLOPS 3.5e22 vs 3.1e23
  setup: de-biased inference using 4 cyclic permutations; Atlas fine-tunes while the baselines use in-context learning
  quote: "For the 5-shot setting,Atlas outperforms GPT-3 by 4%, while using 15× less parameters, and 10× less pre-training compute."
  where: p.13, Table 7 p.14
- claim: Against retrieval-in-the-prompt with Gopher and Google Search, Atlas matches the score with far less compute.
  number: 38.7 EM vs 38.4 (Ensemble) / 32.7 (RAG)
  setup: NQ 15-shot with 50 passages
  quote: "Atlas, using the same 15 training examples and 50 passages achieves 38.7 EM, despite having 25× fewer parameters, and requiring comparatively negligible compute."
  where: p.14
- claim: Product quantisation cuts index memory about 10x with negligible loss.
  number: 49GB to 4GB (Wikipedia); 587GB to 50GB (combined)
  setup: Atlas-3B, 64-shot NQ, fp16 exact-search baseline
  quote: "the Wikipedia index can be compressed from 49GB to 4GB with negligible drop in retrieval precision and exact match."
  where: p.18
- claim: Leakage of MMLU questions into the CCNet index is small, and filtering it costs little.
  number: 2.8% leaked; 56.4 to 55.8
  setup: n-gram overlap of at least 75% of the question length, checked manually
  quote: "The MMLU score drops slightly when controlling for this leakage from 56.4 to 55.8% (-.5%)."
  where: p.17
- claim: Gains from scaling the reader level off with full data but not at 64 shots.
  number: 3B to 11B: +0.6 NQ full vs +3.7 NQ 64-shot
  setup: Dec 2018 Wikipedia index, Table 19
  quote: "limited gains when scaling from 3B to 11B parameters (+0.6% on NaturalQuestions, +0.5% on TriviaQA). While performance improves substantially when scaling from 3B to 11B parameters with 64 training samples, with +3.7%"
  where: p.29

LIMITS
- The comparison with large LLMs is fine-tuning against in-context prompting. That is a different method as well as a different scale.
- The retriever-loss ablation is a single run at 3B on three tasks, with no error bars. The authors themselves say the differences are not systematic.
- Only the MMLU 5-shot experiment was repeated (5 runs, std 0.5 on the aggregate, up to 20% on single domains). Every other number is a single run.
- The temporal test is small (806 test questions) and templated (TempLAMA cloze).
- Main-table results use the first run only: "we quote the result obtained with our first run."
- MMLU leakage estimates cover CCNet only, and the authors concede that LLMs trained on much larger corpora probably see more leakage.
- There is no study of deleting facts or of conflicts between retrieved and parametric knowledge beyond the TempLAMA swap.
- No latency or serving-cost measurement beyond FLOP estimates and index memory.
- Dated: the baselines are 2022 models (PaLM, Chinchilla, GPT-3), and the reader is an encoder-decoder FiD model, not a decoder-only chat LLM.
- Internal inconsistencies:
  - The abstract says "50x fewer parameters", but the Discussion says PaLM "required 50x more pre-training compute".
  - The text gives MMLU full/transfer as "65.6%", but Table 7 shows 66.0 and Table 6 shows 65.8.
  - Leakage "-.5%" is actually 0.6 points.

BUILDS ON: Contriever (Izacard et al., 2022), MoCo (He et al., 2020), Fusion-in-Decoder (Izacard & Grave, 2020), attention distillation (Izacard & Grave, 2021), EMDR2 (Sachan et al., 2021), T5 / text-to-text (Raffel et al., 2019), REALM (Guu et al., 2020) and RAG (Lewis et al., 2020) for joint latent-variable training, query-side fine-tuning (Guu et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2021b), DPR (Karpukhin et al., 2020), RETRO (Borgeaud et al., 2021), kNN-LM (Khandelwal et al., 2020), PQ (Jégou et al., 2011), memory-efficient ODQA (Izacard et al., 2020), TempLAMA (Dhingra et al., 2022), KILT (Petroni et al., 2020), MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021), CCNet (Wenzek et al., 2020).

CODE: none. These are the prompt templates (Appendix):
- QA, p.29: "question: {question text} answer: [MASK_0]" → "[MASK_0] {answer} ."
- MMLU, p.27: "question: {question text}\noptions: (A) {answer 1 text} (B) {answer 2 text} (C) {answer 3 text} (D) {answer 4 text}\nanswer: [MASK_0]"
- Index-refresh overhead formula, p.6: "N×Pretr / 4×B×K×Plm×R"

FIGURES:
- Top candidate is Table 11, p.18 (a table, not a figure): a 2x2 of train year by index year, closed-book vs Atlas. It makes the swap-the-index point faster than prose. It is easy to redraw.
- Figure 1, p.2: "uses retrieval during both pre-training and fine-tuning". One example flows through the MLM, QA and fact-check tasks. This is a good architecture overview for the "train retriever and reader jointly" idea.
- Figure 4, p.19: index compression, recall@50 and EM against memory. Useful only if the note covers index cost.
- Figure 3, p.16: MMLU retrieval sources and the effect of answer frequency. Not central to the note.

PROBLEMS:
- Ligature artifacts in the extraction ("ﬁ", "eﬀ").
- Rows run together in Table 11 ("1.52020" means 1.5, then the row for the 2020 index). I reconstructed them as 2017 answers / 2020 index = 12.1, 10.2, 2.9, 53.1, and 2020 answers / 2017 index = 4.8, 50.1, 3.6, 4.2, which matches the prose.
- Equations come out flattened in the text.
- No embedded instructions found.
